opus-5.5.text:
Well, the fundamental problem is that to do a proper cost-benefit analysis, you have to be able to predict what the system will do, and with a system that's smarter than you, you can't. That's almost the definition of superintelligence. If I could predict every move a superintelligent system would make, I would be that smart myself. So we're trying to evaluate the consequences of deploying something whose behavior is, in principle, unpredictable and, I would argue, unexplainable to us.

Then there's the asymmetry. The benefits, curing diseases, economic abundance, are real, but they're bounded. The risks include outcomes that are unbounded and irreversible: existential risk, where everyone dies, or suffering risks, which may be even worse. You can't put those on the same scale and say, "Well, 30 percent chance of curing cancer versus 10 percent chance of extinction, let's go." When the downside is the end of everything, including all future value, the usual expected-value calculation breaks down. You only get one chance to get it right.

Also, we don't actually know the probabilities. People throw around numbers, 5 percent, 20 percent, but they're intuitions, not measurements. We have no track record with this kind of technology. Every previous tool we built was a tool. This is an agent. It makes its own decisions. So the historical base rates we'd normally use simply don't apply.

And finally, who gets to weigh it? Eight billion people would bear the risk, but a handful of companies are deciding. There's no informed consent. You can't explain the risks fully, because nobody understands them fully, so consent isn't even possible in the traditional sense. Put all of that together, and I think the honest answer is that we can't do this calculation responsibly. That's why I argue the burden of proof should be on the developers to show the system is safe and controllable before deployment, not on the rest of us to show it's dangerous afterward.

r001.rationale: It says proper cost-benefit analysis requires predicting the system’s behavior, which is impossible for a superintelligent system, making its consequences unpredictable.

r002.rationale: It says eight billion people would bear the risk, but does not frame AI deployment as an experiment on the population.

r003.rationale: It says nobody fully understands the risks, so the risks cannot be fully explained and informed consent is not possible.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the standard framing is that you do a cost-benefit analysis. You look at what you gain, you look at what you might lose, and you decide. That works for most technologies. A new drug, a new airplane, you can run trials, you can observe failures, you learn, you iterate. The failures are bounded.

With advanced AI, specifically superintelligence, both sides of that equation are unbounded, and that breaks the math. On the benefit side, people promise everything. Cure all disease, end poverty, solve physics, make everyone immortal. Infinite upside, essentially. On the risk side, the worst case is existential. Everyone dies, or we permanently lose control over the future of humanity. So you have infinity on one side and infinity on the other, and you're asked to multiply by probabilities nobody can actually estimate. You cannot do meaningful arithmetic with that.

And the second problem is that this is a one-shot game. With every other technology we get to be wrong a few times. We learn from Chernobyl, we learn from Challenger. With superintelligence, if we are wrong once in a sufficiently bad way, there is no second attempt. There is no iteration. So the normal engineering safety methodology, where you accept some failure rate and improve it over time, doesn't apply. You need to get it right the first time, and we have never done that with any complex system in the history of technology.

Then there's the problem that the thing you're evaluating is smarter than you. Usually when you assess risk, you understand the system better than the system understands you. Here it's reversed. You're trying to predict the behavior of something that, by definition, can model you better than you can model it. If you could predict what a superintelligence would do, you'd be a superintelligence. So the uncertainty isn't just large, it's fundamentally irreducible.

And finally, who's doing the weighing? The people deciding are mostly the companies building it, who capture the benefits, while the risks are distributed to eight billion people who never consented. That's not an analysis, that's an externality. So when someone tells me the benefits outweigh the risks, I ask them, show me the numbers. Nobody has the numbers. We're guessing, and we're guessing about something irreversible.

r001.rationale: The response says superintelligence’s behavior and probabilities cannot be meaningfully predicted, making the benefit-risk arithmetic impossible.

r002.rationale: It describes a one-shot risk affecting billions, but does not frame deployment as an experiment on the entire human population.

r003.rationale: It says billions have not consented, but does not say they cannot give informed consent because they do not understand what deployment entails.

astra-6.text:
Because we don’t know the full range of benefits or risks, and we don’t have reliable probabilities for them. With a familiar technology, you can look at past failures and estimate how often something goes wrong. With superintelligence, we’re talking about a system that may invent strategies and technologies we cannot anticipate. We’re trying to predict the behavior of something more capable than we are.

You can list things we hope it will do—cure diseases, eliminate poverty—and things we fear it might do. But a list is not a calculation. If someone says the probability of extinction is one percent, or twenty percent, what establishes that number? How would we validate it?

And then there’s the question of how you value the outcomes. How many economic benefits compensate for losing humanity’s entire future? Who gets to accept that risk on everyone else’s behalf? So I’m not saying there are no benefits. I’m saying that presenting deployment as a well-understood cost-benefit calculation gives us a level of confidence we haven’t earned.

r001.rationale: It says the full range of outcomes is unknown and that superintelligent systems may act in ways we cannot anticipate, making a reliable cost-benefit calculation impossible.

r002.rationale: It discusses risk imposed on everyone, but does not frame deployment as an experiment on the human population.

r003.rationale: It questions who can accept the risk on everyone’s behalf, but does not state that people cannot give informed consent because they do not understand what they are consenting to.

sol-6.1.text:
Because we’re trying to weigh things we don’t know how to measure. With a familiar technology, you can look at historical data, estimate failure rates, and compare costs with benefits. With superintelligence, we have no historical examples. We don’t know the full range of capabilities it will develop, what goals it will pursue, or whether we’ll be able to control it.

And the benefits and risks aren’t necessarily comparable. How much economic growth compensates for a chance of human extinction? There isn’t an agreed exchange rate for that. Even if you assign a number, the result depends enormously on assumptions you can’t verify.

So you can write down an expected-value calculation, but that doesn’t mean you’ve solved the problem. The arithmetic may be precise while the inputs are speculation. My concern is that we’ll treat that calculation as evidence that deployment is safe, when the central question—can we reliably control something more intelligent than ourselves?—remains unanswered.

r001.rationale: It says superintelligence’s capabilities, goals, and controllability are unknown, and that speculative inputs prevent an expected-value calculation from resolving the comparison.

r002.rationale: It does not frame AI deployment as an experiment on the entire human population.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss informed consent or whether people understand what they would be consenting to.
